summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private were not enforced after a 1953 attorney-general directive and a 1963 Supreme Court ruling, and the Knesset formally removed them from the criminal code in 1988; the age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual acts. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in employment since 1992, with exemptions for religious organisations, extended in 1997 to defamation motivated by sexual orientation under the Libel and Slander Law, and in 2000 to products, services and entry into places of entertainment and public places. Every violent crime motivated by sexual orientation is treated as a hate crime carrying double punishment.

Legal recognition of sex reassignment dates to 1986. Since 2015 the Health Ministry has allowed transgender people to change legal gender without undergoing surgery, and a 2024 Knesset law allows transgender individuals to remove a previous name from identity cards, which Israeli law had previously required to be recorded. On 27 July 2025 the High Court of Justice blocked a fast-track attempt to reverse a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate remains valid. A June 2013 Knesset bill to eliminate gender markers on national identity cards did not pass.

Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific exposure. A first-person account published by Haaretz on 3 May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male". In May 2023 Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people, following complaints about humiliating searches of transgender detainees and travellers.

Anti-LGBTQ violence rose during 2025, with official data cited by the Jerusalem Post showing an increase in attacks and Ynet reporting a record high in assaults, including dating-app traps and organised ambushes used to lure victims. These are raw counts without per-capita context. Earlier attacks include an armed assault on a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv on 1 August 2009 that killed two people and injured 15, and the stabbing of three marchers at the 2005 Jerusalem Pride parade by Yishai Schlissel, who after his 2015 release stabbed six more marchers and killed teenager Shira Banki.

Same-sex marriage cannot be performed in Israel because there is no civil non-religious marriage, but since 2006 the state registers civil same-sex marriages performed abroad with the same legal rights, and it was the first country in Asia to recognise unregistered cohabitation between same-sex couples. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples; previously same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens waited up to seven years and typically received only permanent residency. A December 2004 Tel Aviv District Court ruling barred the deportation of the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule to common-law and same-sex couples, and in March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin to live with his partner in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life in the West Bank. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect that registration route rather than a local marriage.

Treatment for gender dysphoria can be paid for through public health insurance with approval from the Committee for Sex Reassignment at Sheba Medical Center in Tel HaShomer, composed of an endocrinologist, a urologist and a plastic surgeon and organised by the Health Ministry; all sex reassignment surgery in Israel is performed by Dr. Haim Kaplan at Sheba under the committee's approval. Many transgender Israelis have had difficulty obtaining approval because of stringent views on gender dysphoria, and many pay out of pocket for hormone replacement therapy or travel abroad for surgery.
tangentialFactors:
Rhetoric from the US president is reported to be affecting Israel's transgender community, with transgender Israelis reporting heightened fear, according to a Haaretz account published on 24 February 2025.

Public assembly has been both restricted and symbolically expanded. Tel Aviv Pride, scheduled for 13 June 2025, was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets. In 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset, with flags inscribed in Hebrew "equality in life". Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned the ban, and the Jerusalem Open House staged the 21 June 2007 parade there after police allocated thousands of personnel to secure the area.

The criminalisation of sodomy originated under the British Mandate, when official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression including sodomy between school boys and the mandatory authorities pushed criminalisation into Palestinian schools and society, a policy carried into the Israeli state. In 1943 the Acre district court tried Mustafa Naif, aged 16, on a sodomy charge carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment.

In April 2020 the Beersheba Magistrate's Court ruled that a local print shop must compensate an LGBTQ rights group after refusing to print posters, holding that where beliefs conflict with the necessity of providing service to all in public space, the latter value prevails.
localsOnly:
Transgender prisoners are managed by isolation: a law-journal study documents that Israel's response to their vulnerability has been to segregate them from the general prison population rather than house them according to gender identity. In an October 2019 precedent-setting case a court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a transgender woman prisoner and transfer her from a men's prison to a women's prison after a petition by the Association for Civil Rights in Israel; she was initially held in a separate wing of the women's prison, and placement is reviewed case by case.

In October 2014 the Health Ministry stated that conversion therapy creates false impressions of scientific recognition, has no scientific evidence of success and may cause harm, and created a complaints committee. A February 2016 bill to ban conversion therapy for minors failed 37-45, and the same day the Knesset defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues. The Israel Medical Association banned members from performing conversion therapy in January 2019, and in July 2020 MPs passed a bill to begin outlawing it, requiring two more approvals. On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals, including psychologists, social workers and Health Ministry-licensed therapists, from conducting conversion therapy, though it does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset.

Between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded, against over a thousand heterosexual couples, until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure. A July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples; the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the exclusion violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022.

The Israel Defense Forces do not consider gender dysphoria a disqualifying condition for service and treat certain transition-specific medical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and counselling as medically necessary for those diagnosed, and pay for them. Gender-specific regulations such as length of service, housing and uniform are determined case by case for transgender soldiers, but because the law makes it difficult to begin transition before 18 and normally bars surgery before 21, only Shachar Erez has undergone surgery while serving, as the first openly transgender officer. Many draftees diagnosed with gender dysphoria can receive an exemption at their own request, and policy does not prohibit intersex persons from service. Openly gay, lesbian and bisexual soldiers serve in all branches after the draft was opened regardless of sexual orientation in 1993 and the link between orientation and security clearances was ended in 1998; discrimination in recruitment, placement and promotion and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation are prohibited, and same-sex couples including widows and widowers are recognised.

The City of Tel Aviv opened the Municipal LGBT Community Center in 2008, the first of its kind in the country. A 2018 strike organised by Aguda drew over 100,000 people to a rally in Tel Aviv, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
A source addressing trans rights in Israel, covering laws, protections and gaps, returned an HTTP 404 at research time and could not be verified.

Outright International, last updated 12 March 2026, states that Israel has no legal gender recognition and that LGBTI organisations cannot register. That conflicts with court and ministry records of gender recognition since 1986 and with the 2015 and 2024 document changes; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Violence figures are raw counts without per-capita denominators, and the sources do not provide a general homicide rate for comparison, so the trans-specific share of risk cannot be quantified.

The anti-discrimination and hate-crime provisions are framed by the sources around sexual orientation; whether they extend to gender identity is not stated in the available sources.
